item.content:encoded:
The best time of the baseball year is finally here. The playoffs begin Tuesday, with a quadruple-header of wild-card games on tap. The schedule for each series' first two games is identical.
Let's break down how each team got here, how they can win, X-factors, series predictions and more before the wild-card round begins.
AL: CWS-HOU • BOS-NYY | NL: PHI-ATL • CHC-SD
No. 6 Philadelphia Phillies vs. No. 3 Atlanta Braves
Projected starters
(all times ET)
Game 1, 2 p.m. Tuesday (NBC/PCK): Jesús Luzardo (PHI) vs. Chris Sale (ATL)
Game 2, 2 p.m. Wednesday (NBC/PCK): Cristopher Sánchez (PHI) vs. Tyler Mahle (ATL)
Game 3, TBD*: Aaron Nola (or Zack Wheeler on four days' rest) (PHI) vs. Grant Holmes (ATL)
(*if necessary)
How they got here
Phillies: It was a Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde type of season for the Phillies, to say the least. For the second time in five seasons, an in-season managerial firing was needed to light a fire under an underperforming veteran roster that appeared to be letting their window close. But the Phillies, like they've done before, found a way to get themselves going on the back of their starting rotation. The Phillies didn't make it easy on themselves in September, going 10-14 down the stretch and needing to win their regular-season finale against the Rays to punch their ticket to the postseason. But now that they're in, this veteran group will look to show that they're better than the past month suggests.
Braves: It was a reassuring year in Atlanta, a much-needed reminder that no, this era of Braves baseball was not over after their disastrous, postseason-less 2025. A change in manager, from the now-retired Brian Snitker to the endearingly pugnacious Walt Weiss, set the tone. As did a major refresh of Atlanta's coaching staff. That turnover, in contrast with the continuity on the roster, proved crucial as Atlanta waltzed to its first division title since 2023.
Big campaigns from metronomic first baseman Matt Olson and 2025 NL Rookie of the Year Drake Baldwin shocked nobody. The same was true for ace Chris Sale, certain to be voted an NL Cy Young finalist. But few would've predicted Michael Harris II leading the team in bWAR with a dynamic, consistent offensive season. Role players such as Mauricio Dubón, Mike Yastrzemski and Dominic Smith all delivered critical production to help offset underwhelming seasons from the likes of Ozzie Albies and Austin Riley.
Ronald Acuña Jr., that wonderfully mercurial burst of baseballing light, might've fit into that last group if not for an otherworldly September in which he clocked seven homers with a .950 OPS. That renaissance continuing into October would be a game-changer for the Braves, whose 2021 title came with Acuña sidelined.
X-factors
Phillies: Trea Turner
The regular season wasn't kind to shortstop Trea Turner, who recorded the worst season of his career. But the thing about the postseason is that it allows players who have not yet written the final story on their season to become heroes. And if the Phillies want to move past Atlanta and reach the NLDS for the fifth straight year, Turner finding his rhythm would be a welcomed sight for the team's offense. Turner has a .733 OPS off Sale in 25 career at-bats and a very respectable .863 OPS off Mahle in 25 career at-bats.
Braves: Tyler Mahle
Chris Sale is going to start Game 1 for Atlanta, and he's probably going to be pretty good. That feels as bankable as anything in our topsy-turvy world. But Mahle, set to throw Game 2, has been one of the game's most reliable starters since he joined the Braves from a zip-less San Francisco team at the deadline. The veteran righty posted a 1.99 ERA with Atlanta, allowing one earned or fewer in seven of his nine starts.
Mahle's most recent start, however, was a relative stinker. He surrendered five runs and struck out just four at home against an undermanned Reds lineup. And the underlying metrics, it should be said, are a bit more skeptical about Mahle's prospects. That's understandable. He doesn't throw that hard or strike out oodles of hitters. He hasn't conjured more swing-and-miss or meaningfully lowered opponents' hard-hit rate as a Brave. And yet, Mahle has found a way to find outs. Whether he can do so against Philly's bats will be huge.
How they win
Phillies: Can any team in baseball go toe-to-toe with Philly's starting rotation? With the quartet of Wheeler, Sánchez, Luzardo and Nola, the Phillies should have the advantage in a three-, five- or seven-game series. So while their offense is more of a wild card (pun intended), this team should be able to count on its starter giving them a chance to win every time out. And if that foursome gets hot, it's not outlandish to believe they could carry Philly on another deep postseason run.
Braves: It has been a restful week for the Braves, who were able to sit back, relax and line up their starting rotation for this wild-card series. The same cannot be said for Philly, which needed every last out to clinch on the regular season's final day. For the Phillies, the sense of exhaustion is real and gives Atlanta a legitimate advantage.
But it all starts with Sale. If he cruises like he's capable of in Game 1, that puts Atlanta in the catbird seat. Only one team in the current playoff format (the 2025 Yankees) came back to win a wild-card series after losing the first game.
Series prediction: Braves in 3
No. 6 Chicago White Sox vs. No. 3 Houston Astros
Projected starters
(all times ET)
Game 1, 5 p.m. ET Tuesday (PCK/NBCSN): David Sandlin (CWS) vs. Peter Lambert (HOU)
Game 2 5 p.m. ET Wednesday (PCK/NBCSN): Sean Burke (CWS) vs. Hunter Brown (HOU)
Game 3, TBD*: Davis Martin (CWS) vs. Hayden Wesneski (HOU)
(*if necessary)
How they got here
White Sox: The White Sox have been easily one of the best stories of the 2026 regular season, reaching the postseason for the first time since 2021. Chicago became the first team in MLB history to reach the postseason following three consecutive 100-loss seasons, capturing the third AL wild-card spot. The offense, led by first-time All-Stars Miguel Vargas and Munetaka Murakami, was the driving force behind the Sox's success. Chicago finished the season with a top-five offense in MLB.
The fact that the White Sox didn't win the AL Central might come as a disappointment, considering they were in first place for the majority of the second half. Still, it's undeniable that any result that puts them in the playoffs is a huge victory for the organization and a fan base that has been waiting for competitive baseball.
Astros: For a franchise that has accomplished so much over the past decade, there's something shameful, even humiliating about raising the 2026 AL West banner. That's because these Astros are, by record, the single worst division winner in the sport's long past. Before Sunday, no team with a .500 record or below had ever reached the postseason. But Houston rewrote history thanks to an MVP-caliber season from Yordan Alvarez and a tidal wave of mediocrity from its AL West counterparts. Their inclusion in the October jamboree is more an indictment of the Texas Rangers and the Seattle Mariners than anything else, but the Astros at least ended on a high note with their 9-0 win over the A's on Sunday.
Houston also deserves a morsel of credit for refurbishing its season after a disastrous April. Reaching .500 with the fourth-worst starting staff by ERA — only the Reds, A's and Rockies were worse — is also an accomplishment worth commending, a testament to something. Where would this club be without Peter Lambert, whose 3.87 ERA in 153 2/3 innings offered the only semblance of stability for a roster constantly in flux?
Things got sad enough, discombobulated enough, that in August owner Jim Crane relieved GM Dana Brown of his duties. There's an overwhelming expectation that skipper Joe Espada won't be back next year, either. It's difficult to be optimistic about Houston's very uncertain future. But in the random present of playoff baseball, anything is possible — especially when you employ the best hitter on the planet.
X-factors
White Sox: Munetaka Murakami
Munetaka Murakami is a game-changer, and his presence in the White Sox's lineup is a huge advantage in the postseason. The White Sox's rookie slugger burst onto the scene in 2026, hitting 35 home runs and providing instant impact in his first season after coming over from Japan. But following a midseason hamstring injury, the league seemed to adjust to him; Murakami finished with a slashline of .184/.328/.423 and 11 homers since Aug 1. Still, he has the type of power that can change a series by himself, and with three homers in the final week of the season, he appears to be coming out of his second-half slump. If Murakami has rediscovered his power stroke, it could change this series.
Astros: Isaac Paredes
Yordan Alvarez is currently the best hitter on earth. He cannot, under any circumstances, be allowed to dictate proceedings during this series. Chicago must make somebody else in Houston's mediocre lineup beat them. If there's a base open with Alvarez up, he should just stroll straight to first every time.
That puts a mountain of pressure on Paredes. The stocky third baseman has been hitting right behind Alvarez for most of the season and has, for the most part, showed well. He's a supremely weird hitter, one who rarely hits the ball hard or barrels it up. But Paredes doesn't whiff, doesn't punch out and has a preternatural knack for pulling the ball in the air. Expect him to come up multiple times in big spots with runners on.
How they win
White Sox: The White Sox's offense has carried them all season, and if they hope to advance to the ALDS against their division rival, they'll have to slug their way there. Vargas, Murakami and shortstop Colson Montgomery each finished the season with more than 30 longballs, and the Sox finished fifth in MLB in homers. For a team built to slug, Daikin Park in Houston isn't the worst environment to play in on the road. Chicago's power-packed lineup has shown that if they're hitting the ball out of the ballpark, offensively, they can play with anyone.
Astros: Houston desperately needs offensive contributions from someone besides Alvarez. Maybe it's the aforementioned Paredes or the en fuego Yainer Díaz. Perhaps Jose Altuve, 36 years old and in full decline, has one magical month left in his Hall of Fame career. But with such a tattered pitching staff, the Astros need to score to win. They also need to win the Hunter Brown start; he's far and away their best starter. They need a lot, frankly. And yet, much weirder October things have happened inside that East Texas thunderdome over the past decade.
Series prediction: Astros in 3
No. 5 Boston Red Sox vs. No. 4 New York Yankees
Projected starters
(all times ET)
Game 1, 8 p.m. Tuesday (NBC/PCK): Payton Tolle (BOS) vs. Cam Schlittler (NYY)
Game 2, 8 p.m. Wednesday (NBC/PCK): Sonny Gray (BOS) vs. Max Fried (NYY)
Game 3, TBD*: Ranger Suárez (BOS) vs. Gerrit Cole (NYY)
(*if necessary)
How they got here
Red Sox: Odysseus would be proud. What a winding, bizarre and tumultuous road it has been for the Sox. Boston began the year like a snail on Unisom, posting a lackluster 9-17 record through April 24. That precipitated a dramatic, Red Wedding-style culling, in which manager Alex Cora and several other staff members were relieved of their duties. Extended injury list stints for the team's two most important pieces, outfielder Roman Anthony and 2025 Cy Young runner-up Garrett Crochet, made a turnaround feel awfully unlikely. On July 24, the Sox lost a rubber match in Colorado and traveled home 14 games under .500. Their postseason odds wallowed around 10%.
Then, everything changed. It began with a home mop against the Yanks and fully kicked into gear when the Red Sox hit the road for a three-city swing the first week of July. They went 9-0 on that trip before winning six straight at home. That 15-game streak catapulted them back into contention and the good graces of an understandably unplugged fan base. Between July 3 and Aug. 7, the Sox went a ridiculous 32-5, trampolining from 14 games under .500 to 13 games over. Fenway was a zoo. Nothing could go wrong. Boston ballfans beamed once again.
The heater earned Cora's replacement, Chad Tracy, the full-time gig. It also afforded the Sox a relatively comfortable September. It's worth noting, though, that Boston has not played particularly crisply since cooling off from the volcanic run, with a 21-22 record since Aug. 8. Ultimately, their final numbers and standing in the American League are not shocking or unexpected, even though Boston's odyssey was wonky beyond comparison.
Yankees: For all the stress, the drama, the hand-wringing, for all the injuries and under-performance, 2026 was a relatively straightforward season in YankeeLand. A lot, it should be said, went wrong. Reigning AL MVP Aaron Judge has played just seven games since May. Giancarlo Stanton hasn't played since April. Max Fried and Carlos Rodón each missed about two months. Young players such as Anthony Volpe, Jasson Dominguez and Austin Wells regressed offensively. Gerrit Cole, coming back from Tommy John, didn't fully recapture his frontline best.
And yet, here the Yankees are, with 93 wins and in an identical place to where they finished last year. That's thanks to breakout campaigns from homegrown pieces such as Cam Schlittler (the AL Cy Young favorite) and Ben Rice (41 home runs and a .897 OPS). Closer David Bednar has been dynamite. Cody Bellinger has been a rock. Skipper Aaron Boone kept the train on the tracks. Three games at home against the Red Sox await. Beyond that looms an ALDS against a daunting division foe. We've been here before.
The largest difference, of course, is the uncertainty swirling around Judge. The Yankees' captain missed three months due to a rib problem, came back for a week, strained his calf and went back on the shelf. Boone says he's preparing for a wild-card round without Judge. Judge says he plans to play. What sort of magic this reduced version of Judge can conjure is easily the juiciest storyline ahead of this rivalry showdown. That said, this series, like this Yankees season, is probably going to be dictated by the pitchers.
X-factors
Red Sox: Roman Anthony
It has been an odd season for the 22-year-old, who missed last year's wild-card festivities due to injury. In March, Anthony was a late addition to Team USA's WBC roster. He shined on that grand stage, impressing his more established teammates and earning plaudits from a coaching staff of hardball lifers. That only ratcheted up the hype on a player expected to carry a franchise less than a year after he became legally permitted to drink a beer.
So when Anthony started slowly, disappointment bubbled. Then, on May 4, he tore a ligament in his finger; that kept him out of action until Aug. 30. A lot happened in the interim, most of which Anthony spent rehabbing at the team's complex in Florida. Since returning, he has looked promising, tantalizingly close to unleashing the full assortment of his talents upon the league. Now, with Willson Contreras banged up and either unavailable or restricted, the pressure returns to Anthony's young shoulders.
Yankees: Luis García Jr.
García was a curious character for the Yankees to shape their trade deadline around. Instead of acquiring a piece that filled an obvious void (righty stick with defensive value or versatility), GM Brian Cashman opted to add the most dynamic hitter possible. New York landed on García, who was in the midst of an offensive breakout under a new Washington Nationals regime.
For a month, that plan bore fruit, with the Dominican slugger posting an .846 OPS in August. But since then, the wheels have fallen off, with García's chase rate skyrocketing. His September OPS started with a 5. He has homered just twice since Aug. 26. He doesn't have an extra-base hit since Sept. 10. There's a chance, given Boston's bevy of southpaws and New York's DH surplus, that he doesn't start every game. But García will get his chances, and whether he comes up big might swing the series.
How they win
Red Sox: Boston's pitching staff is the only one in baseball that ranks in the top five in both home run rate and walk rate. That's a rare combo. Usually, throwing the ball in the strike zone more often leads to more hard contact. But these Red Sox hurlers, for whatever reason, have threaded that needle perfectly. No team in the league has allowed fewer homers. However, no team has hit more than the Yankees. Boston revitalized its season behind pitching and defense, keeping the scores low and the games close. Doing so here will give them the best chance of authoring an upset.
Yankees: No American League team can compete with New York's starting staff. But the Yankees need more than dominance from Schlittler, Fried and Cole. They need length. The bridge to Bednar is unsteady. So the longer the starters go, the rosier that path looks. Offensively, the Yankees need a big swing or two from their right-handed bats against Boston's left-handed arms. That could come from a banged-up Judge or Stanton. It could come from veteran southpaw-killer Paul Goldschmidt, trade-acquisition Heliot Ramos or rookie shortstop George Lombard Jr. If it comes from the beleaguered Anthony Volpe, the tri-state area will lose its collective marbles. But somebody, anybody who stands on the right side of the batter's box has to make an impact.
Series prediction: Yankees in 3
No. 5 Chicago Cubs vs. No. 4 San Diego Padres
(all times ET)
Projected starters
Game 1, 10 p.m. Tuesday (PCK/NBCSN): Shota Imanaga (CHC) vs. Michael King (SD)
Game 2, 10 p.m. Wednesday (PCK/NBCSN): Clay Holmes (CHC) vs. Nick Pivetta (SD)
Game 3, TBD*: Matthew Boyd (CHC) vs. Walker Buehler or Casey Mize or Robbie Ray (SD)
(*if necessary)
How they got here
Cubs: It was Pete Crow-Armstrong's world, and the rest of us just lived in it. Chicago's 24-year-old center fielder went fully supersonic this year, cranking 45 homers, swiping 41 bags and delivering a .945 OPS with his typically elite outfield defense. He will win the NL MVP, and it might be unanimous. That performance shaped and guided and defined this Cubs' season, electrifying an offense that led baseball in OPS, K/BB rate and runs per game.
Alex Bregman's arrival via free agency, too, cannot be understated. He struggled mightily for the first few months, with his extended schneid at one point eliciting boos from a frustrated Wrigley crowd. But since July 12, Bregman leads all qualified National League hitters in OPS. His experience, comportment and leadership, by all accounts, have also had a meaningful impact on Crow-Armstrong.
But pitching woes, in both the rotation and the bullpen, kept Chicago from ever seriously threatening the Brewers for the NL Central title. The Cubs started the year on something of a roller coaster, with two 10-game winning streaks and a 10-game losing streak before the calendar flipped to June. They'll enter October on something of an ice floe, with 15 runs scored in their final six contests.
Padres: San Diego has the best record in baseball since July 24. The day before, the Pads lost a rubber match in Atlanta to fall to three games under. 500. That pushed the club four games adrift of a wild-card spot, with the Cardinals, Pirates, Marlins, Nationals and Diamondbacks standing between them and a trip to October. That was the low-water mark for this team.
Since that date, the Padres have gone 41-18. They won five straight in late July, six straight in August and eight straight in September. They've lost thrice since Labor Day. The reason for the resurgence? Check out these numbers.
| Padres offensive ranks before and after July 24 | | |
| | Before | After |
| Runs/game | 4.14 (25th) | 4.95 (3rd) |
| AVG | .230 (28th) | .268 (2nd) |
| OBP | .307 (27th) | .339 (2nd) |
| SLG | .383 (27th) | .425 (2nd) |
| OPS | .689 (26th) | .764 (2nd) |
San Diego's offense went from bottom-five to top-five. Some of that is batted-ball luck and sequencing. A lot of it is Fernando Tatis Jr. turning back into a monster. Jackson Merrill had a similar rebirth. Ty France continued his bounce-back campaign. Xander Bogaerts shifted from unwatchable to capable. Unsung heroes such as Dustin Harris and Luis Rengifo got hot. The starting pitching did just enough. The game's best bullpen never stopped dominating. It's that unit, led by a cadre of flamethrowers in Mason Miller, Adrian Morejon and Bradgley Rodriguez, that makes these Padres a particularly formidable October opponent.
X-factors
Cubs: Alex Bregman — specifically, his face
One week ago, Bregman was the victim of some very painful misfortune. A check-swing foul ball off the bat of Cubs first baseman Michael Busch struck Bregman in the face while he was standing in the on-deck circle. Blood dripped from below his left eye as he scurried down the dugout steps into the clubhouse. A trip to the hospital revealed multiple facial fractures. The incident kept Bregman out of the lineup until Friday, when he went 0-for-4 with a strikeout as Chicago's DH. He went 4-for-4 with two home runs and a walk in Sunday's season finale.
There's no doubt that Bregman, the textbook definition of a "grinder," will take the field in October. But at what level? He has been so integral to Chicago's lineup for the past few months that even a slightly reduced version of Bregman could unsettle things. Among active players, only his former Astros teammate Jose Altuve has taken more postseason plate appearances.
Padres: Fernando Tatis Jr.
Nothing is more meaningfully different about this year's Padres team compared to the one that went three and see-ya at Wrigley in 2025 than Fernando Tatis Jr.'s stunning offensive reemergence. Things didn't start so swimmingly this year for the swaggering outfielder, who needed 55 games to clock his first longball of this season. But since May 30, Tatis' .914 OPS ranks fourth in the NL, and his 4.9 fWAR ranks second in MLB behind only Crow-Armstrong.
This version of Tatis looks a lot like the one who took the baseball world by storm en route to finishing third in NL MVP in 2021. Will that brilliance show up in a small October sample? It usually has throughout the 27-year-old's career; he holds a 1.114 postseason OPS in 70 plate appearances. Tatis, though, has never advanced past the NLDS. Remember, he was in PED timeout when the Padres stampeded to the NLCS in 2022. Could this month be his path back to full-blown superstardom?
How they win
Cubs: The margins were razor thin when these teams lined up in the wild-card round last year, with a highlight reel of web gems from shortstop Dansby Swanson making the difference. Those games, oddly enough, were incredibly low-scoring, with Chicago snagging two 3-1 wins and San Diego edging out a 3-0 win. It's hard to imagine the Cubs and their underwhelming relief group winning that way again, particularly on the road. To advance, they'll need buckets of runs. With PCA, Bregman, Seiya Suzuki and Co., that's a real possibility.
Padres: The Padres' formula for success has been the same for the past few seasons: Shorten the game. San Diego realistically needs five innings from its starters. Then manager Craig Stammen gets to turn things over to the best relief core in baseball, led by southpaw Adrían Morejon and flamethrower Mason Miller. The Friars' starting pitching has gotten stronger as they've gotten healthy, so if Michael King in Game 1 and likely Nick Pivetta in Game 2 can each give San Diego 15 outs, the Padres have a good chance of making quick work of Chicago.

WEST SACRAMENTO, Calif. (AP) — Yordan Alvarez launched a three-run homer and the Houston Astros went deep five times Saturday night as they moved closer to a division title with a 13-2 victory over the Athletics.
Houston (80-81) can clinch the AL West crown and the No. 3 seed in the American League playoffs with another win Sunday over the A’s in their regular-season finale or a Texas Rangers loss at Minnesota. Either team will become the first to win a division with a .500 record or worse, excluding shortened seasons.
Alvarez homered in the fifth inning to put the Astros up 6-1. His 42nd homer of the season tied him with Tampa Bay slugger Junior Caminero for second in the AL.
Houston finished with 16 hits as Jeremy Peña, Isaac Paredes and Jose Altuve combined for nine of them and seven RBIs.
Peña hit a pair of two-run homers, one in the third and the other in the eighth. He finished 4 for 6 with four RBIs. Parades homered in the first to open the scoring and went 3 for 5.
Hayden Wesneski (6-2) threw seven innings and struck out five while allowing six hits and two runs.
The Astros scored six runs, including Lucas Spence’s solo homer, between the seventh and ninth to expand their lead to 13-2.
Jack Perkins (3-13) pitched five innings for the Athletics. He struck out nine but gave up six runs and three homers.
Up next
Neither team had announced a starting pitcher for Sunday’s regular-season finale.

item.content:encoded:
Most of baseball’s awards races are formalities this year. The favorites are clear, and deservedly so. Pete Crow-Armstrong is having one of the greatest seasons of the 21st century. Jacob Misiorowski is a closer throwing starter innings. Bobby Witt Jr. has been terrific, but Yordan Alvarez is unsolvable. Cam Schlittler has more fastballs than batters have answers. Kevin McGonigle is a phenom. But I’m most interested in the sixth major race: National League Rookie of the Year. The gambling odds would tell you that it too is settled, with Sal Stewart the prohibitive favorite. But if I had a vote this year, I’d cast it for JJ Wetherholt, and I want to explain myself because I think this race provides a fascinating look into old school versus new school baseball statistics, and how both have blind spots.
Before we get into my argument, let’s get a few disclaimers out of the way. I am not voting for NL Rookie of the Year. I’m not a member of the BBWAA, even. I haven’t placed any wagers on NL ROY, or on any awards, or on anything even peripherally related to this. I was a Cardinals fan before I started working in baseball, but that has faded away. I have a lot of fond memories of Ozzie Smith, but I’m a fan of the sport now, not a team, and I’ve watched more Reds games than Cardinals games this year because I love watching Elly De La Cruz play. No one in the world is truly unbiased, but I don’t have a horse in this race in any meaningful way.
With that out of the way, let’s get down to brass tacks. The two leading candidates for the award are Stewart and Wetherholt, with Carson Benge a distant-enough third according to the odds that I’m largely leaving him out of the discussion, though he’ll make some cameos. Stewart’s résumé revolves around his thunderous bat. He’s batting .266/.333/.465, with 32 homers and a gaudy 110 RBI. Even in an offense-friendly home park, that’s good for a 115 wRC+, 15th-best among qualifying first basemen, and of course the RBI total is better than that. He’s played so-so defense at first – not that I care much about that in award voting – and has accrued 2.2 WAR per our calculation of the statistic.
If Stewart’s calling card is his power, Wetherholt’s is his lack of weaknesses. He’s hitting .244/.343/.365, good for a 103 wRC+, with 17 homers despite playing his home games in cavernous Busch Stadium. He walks a ton and rarely strikes out. He’s a plus baserunner and an elite defender at second base, where he’s the favorite for a Gold Glove and is sure to draw strong consideration in my Fielding Bible voting. Between his ability to get on base, his baserunning, his defense, and the fact that WAR values second basemen more highly than first basemen for the same batting line, we have him at 4.5 WAR, the best mark among NL rookies. Benge is second on that list at 3.7 WAR; he’s been a better hitter than Wetherholt and a better defender than Stewart.
Great – now let’s throw WAR out the window. When I tell you that one of these players has nearly double the WAR of the other and that the one with the lower WAR total is a favorite to win the award, that should tell you that “but look at the WAR” isn’t a good argument. I’ll mention the building blocks of WAR again in this article, because the building blocks of WAR are “playing baseball” more or less, but the headline number? Banished to the shadow realm.
While “rookie” is exceedingly well defined for the purposes of this award, “of the year” has no obvious qualifications. It’s simply the best rookie-eligible player in each voter’s estimation. That leaves the field wide open, and it means that many different interpretations have merit. My own interpretation is that the award should go to the best-performing rookie, with their expected future production used sparingly as a tiebreaker. If a voter wanted to instead vote for the rookie they thought had the brightest future, though, I wouldn’t argue with them – that’s as much a rookie of the year as my version.
This year, my interpretation means that I need to compare Stewart’s power to Wetherholt’s all-around game. And like I mentioned, we won’t be using WAR to make the decision for us. It’s clearly true that being better at defense is important, and it’s also clearly true that if two players had the same batting line, you’d prefer an average-fielding shortstop over a DH. But I don’t think it’s reasonable to say that Wetherholt was nearly three wins more valuable than Stewart by virtue of position and defense. That’s just too many wins for me to take as gospel. Defensive statistics are noisy. Positional adjustments aren’t set in stone. We’re going to go component-by-component instead.
It’s important to give Stewart appropriate credit for his run production ability, and I don’t think that wRC+ fully captures it. That statistic measures every single plate appearance in a neutral context. That’s very useful for figuring out the future, because hitters don’t control the context they bat in, but it’s less useful for saying how much a hitter helped his team win in the games they actually played.
I don’t think RBI numbers are a very good way of capturing that either, though. It’s immediately obvious that team context has a ton to do with RBI totals. A hitter who batted with the bases loaded every time would have a ludicrous RBI total even if he was terrible; a hitter who always came up with the bases empty could be peak Ted Williams and still put up paltry RBI numbers. Now, those two scenarios aren’t realistic. But leadoff hitters bat with runners on base far less often than cleanup hitters. Teams with poor offenses give their hitters fewer opportunities to drive a run home. Like many statistics, RBI totals reflect a blend of skill, opportunity, and chance – round ball and round bat, as they always say.
Fortunately, there’s a statistic that accounts for opportunity: the clumsily-named RE24. That name sounds like an experimental drug from a sci-fi movie, but it’s actually a straightforward idea. Take the situation before a hitter comes to the plate. Then take the situation after they finish batting, accounting for runs scored, runners advanced, and whether or not they made an out. Turn it all into run expectancy, and give them credit (or assign them blame) for the difference in run-scoring expectation before and after their at-bat.
To put this in more concrete terms, consider a plate appearance that starts with a runner on third and one out. A sacrifice fly moves the expected runs scored in that inning from 0.86 to 1.1, crediting the hitter with 0.24 runs of value. A strikeout drops the expected runs scored that inning from 0.86 to 0.32, docking the hitter 0.54 runs. Or consider a runner on third with two outs. A single moves run scoring expectations from 0.32 to 1.21, a gain of 0.89 runs. A walk, on the other hand, only bumps the run expectancy from 0.32 to 0.48, a gain of 0.16 runs. Want a statistic that says a single is better than a walk when you can drive in a run, or that strikeouts with runners in scoring position are bad? RE24 does the trick. It also handles the other side of the equation well. With the bases empty, a walk really is as good as a single, and RE24 agrees.
By considering the state when a hitter comes to the plate, RE24 accounts for opportunity. All you can do as a hitter is play the hand you’re dealt. RE24 measures “the hand you’re dealt” in a slightly smarter way than just ignoring it completely. I don’t think it’s controversial to say that situational hitting – changing your approach based on the game situation – is a real thing that batters do. RE24 sets the incentives right; it gives you credit for doing the thing that makes your team score the most runs, and by construction “the thing that makes your team score the most runs” is different in different situations.
RE24 thinks Stewart is pretty dang good. It has him 20.3 runs above average this year. In other words, a perfectly league average batter hitting in his spot would have cost the Reds 20-ish runs in one way or another – fewer homers, more strikeouts in big spots, fewer baserunners to open innings, the whole gamut of ways that Stewart has added value this season. Those RBIs are a big part of it. He’s second on his team in RE24 behind De La Cruz (sure, checks out), and second only to TJ Rumfield, who gets to play in Colorado, among qualifying NL rookies. Given that RE24 doesn’t adjust for park, I’m comfortable saying that no NL rookie did more with their bat than Stewart.
Of course, Wetherholt was no slouch offensively either. While Stewart batted second, third, and fourth and cashed in runners in front of him, Wetherholt led off in every game he played this year. His OBP-heavy game is a great fit for how often he came up with the bases empty; when there are no runners to advance, a walk is as good as a hit, and his double-digit walk rate is perfect in that spot. RE24 gives Wetherholt credit for 10.2 runs above average. (Benge is marginally ahead of Wetherholt here at 11.3 runs.)
That’s one estimate of the gap in value between Stewart’s bat and Wetherholt’s bat – 10 to 11 runs. If you’re interested in another, there’s Win Probability Added. Think RE24, but instead of measuring how many runs are likely to score, WPA measures how likely the batting team is to win before and after the plate appearance. No one cares if you hit a grand slam in a 23-3 blowout. A two-run single, down a run in the ninth, is far more valuable to a team’s chances of winning. Why not account for that in our statistics?
WPA thinks that Stewart has added about 1.4 wins to the Reds’ total, as compared to a league average hitter, based on what he’s done in the situations he’s faced. That’s pretty good! Only five rookie hitters in all of baseball have a better mark, and four of them play in the American League. But the fifth member of that group is Wetherholt, who checks in at 1.99 WPA. Though he’s been a worse hitter than Stewart overall, his worst performances have come when there are no stakes. In low-leverage situations, he’s batting a putrid .228/.340/.296, 12% below average. The rest of the time, he’s been 14% above average offensively. In other words, he concentrated his best performances when it mattered most. Stewart, on the other hand, has been steady: very good in high leverage, good in medium leverage, good in low leverage. Benge looks worse by WPA; thanks to some rough performances in big spots, he only gets credit for 0.5 wins.
I don’t think that WPA is a fair measure for evaluating the best rookie, so I would not consider it if I were voting. I mentioned it just in case a voter reading this wanted to take clutchness into account. There’s no evidence that it’s a skill. There’s no evidence that this means Wetherholt will continue to play his best when it matters most. But if you want to give the award to the hitter whose offense was worth the most expected wins at the moment it happened, that would surprisingly be Wetherholt.
I’m much more aligned with RE24’s accounting of the world for this award. I love WPA for awards like MVP that care about “valuable” rather than “best,” and I’m sure I’ll get an article out of that in the long winter we have ahead. I concur that Stewart is a better hitter than Wetherholt, and I think 12 runs is a perfectly reasonable estimate for how much better. He’s been very good in the role the Reds deployed him in, cashing in baserunners. Wetherholt has been good at getting on base to set the table, but Stewart’s bat is clearly more valuable.
One last point on the RBI front: Stewart’s RBI total is impressive, of course, and I don’t think “RBIs don’t matter” is a reasonable dismissal of that. It’s certainly not a way to win an argument. Runs win games, after all. But even if you care a lot about RBIs, you have to adjust them for context. Stewart was 10th in the majors this year when it came to having runners on base when he batted. The top 10 averaged 95 RBI. He did better than that average, but it’s not like his opportunity set didn’t matter. When you bat with so many dudes aboard, you’re going to drive some of them home. We care about how much better he did in the situations he was put into, and 15 extra RBI is no joke, nor are the 21 runs above average that RE24 credits him with. But you can’t just say 110 RBI with no context, because the Reds did a really good job of setting Stewart up with runners on base.
Next, let’s consider baserunning. Wetherholt has stolen 14 bases. Stewart has stolen 15. But Wetherholt is quite efficient, with only one time caught stealing, while Stewart has been gunned down six times. That isn’t good considering that you need to run a 75%-ish success rate on steals to break even. Stewart’s aggression has cost the Reds about half a run compared to just not attempting to steal, while Wetherholt’s attempts have added about 1.5 runs to St. Louis’ ledger.
Excluding steals, Stewart has also cost the Reds on the basepaths. He takes an extra base on just 25% of opportunities, and he’s also made seven outs on the bases this year. Conversely, Wetherholt runs the bases like the leadoff hitter he is. He takes an extra base on 52% of his chances to do so, and he’s only made a single out on the bases this year. That’s an enormous gap. One way of thinking about it? Stewart has been on second base when his team hit a single 11 times this year. He stopped at third five times, scored five times, and got thrown out at home once. Wetherholt has been on second when his team hit a single 20 times this year; he’s stopped at third four times and scored 16 times.
That’s a lot of value that doesn’t show up in the box score. Specifically, if you assign run values to all of that based on how much advancing or making an out changes your team’s scoring expectation, Stewart has been 3.5 runs below average, while Wetherholt has been 1.8 runs above average. Between that and the gap in steals, there’s a seven-run gap in baserunning value between the two. Benge is even a hair better than Wetherholt on the bases, for the record. That passes the sniff test for me; on our leaderboards, Wetherholt and Benge are each one of the best 20 baserunners in baseball this year, while Stewart is one of the 20 worst. But baserunning just isn’t all that important – seven runs of difference is very little. Heck, Yordan Alvarez is a worse baserunner than Stewart and it just doesn’t matter.
The tale of the tape on offense looks like this:
| Metric | Stewart | Wetherholt | Benge |
|---|---|---|---|
| FG Off* | 8.1 | 5.3 | 13.1 |
| RE24 | 20.3 | 10.2 | 11.3 |
| BsR | -3.9 | 3.2 | 3.6 |
| WPA** | 1.35 | 1.99 | 0.53 |
**: denominated in wins, while all other stats are denominated in runs
I think it’s pretty clear that Stewart has been the better player on offense this year, and I think it’s reasonable to think that Benge has been roughly as good as him. I think it’s equally clear that the gap is fairly narrow. Stewart has gotten run-scoring opportunities and cashed them in adroitly. Wetherholt has been a smaller-scale success, but he’s also been good at his role. He leads off and gets on base. We like that, just like we like sluggers who send runners on the basepaths home to celebrate. Wetherholt is also getting it done on the basepaths, while Stewart isn’t. But even though Wetherholt has been one of the best baserunners in baseball and Stewart one of the worst, that gap is smaller than the difference in their production with the bat.
If we were only allowed to consider offensive value, I’d vote for Stewart over Wetherholt. I might vote for Benge over both of them. Considering how many different statistics I looked at that all landed in a similar place, I think the only fair read is that the three are fairly close. All three of these guys were assets to their team on offense, as I’m quite sure that fans of their teams would tell you. But defense matters too, and realistically, this one isn’t as close.
Now, it’s good to remember that defensive metrics are noisy and that you shouldn’t take them as gospel. It’s very hard to measure defensive talent. If someone quotes you an FRV number and tells you that it proves, beyond a doubt, how good a player was with the glove, you have my permission to make a fart noise with your mouth to show them how you feel about it. But let me make some gentle assertions and see what you think about them.
I assert that for the same offensive value, you’d prefer to have a second baseman compared to a first baseman. I don’t think this is particularly controversial. Jose Altuve and Vladimir Guerrero Jr. have very similar career batting lines. Regardless of how you feel about the banging scheme, does anyone think Vlad’s 132 wRC+ at first is more valuable than Altuve’s 127 wRC+ at second? Second basemen aren’t as good of hitters as first basemen! Big league first basemen have a 115 wRC+ this year; big league second basemen have a 95 wRC+ (right fielders are at a 102 wRC+).
The reason for that split is that there’s some minimum defensive level necessary to play second base, and a lot of first basemen don’t clear it. If they did, they’d go play second and improve their team’s offense by a huge amount. I don’t require you to convert that gap into some exact number of wins, but surely, you’ll concede the weak form of my argument – given the same results on offense, a second baseman is more valuable than a first baseman.
Okay, another assertion: JJ Wetherholt is a plus defensive second baseman. Again, I don’t think this is controversial. Every advanced metric says that he’s phenomenal out there. He made only two errors in more than 1,000 innings, the third-lowest mark out of 29 second basemen who played 500 or more innings. He notched 0.48 assists plus putouts per inning – outs per inning, roughly speaking. That’s fifth highest out of that group of 29. He was one of the best at making outs, and also one of the best at avoiding errors. He was first in double plays started per inning, though I’ll give some of that credit to Masyn Winn. He’s the best defensive second baseman by a mile according to Statcast’s FRV, and in the top five according to both DRS and Baseball Prospectus’ RDA. He passes the eye test. He’s the betting favorite to win the NL Gold Glove at second base. You don’t have to put a run value on it to say that Wetherholt has been an excellent fielder at an important defensive position.
One last assertion about defense: Sal Stewart is a middling defender. I’m not trying to say he’s bad. He played across the infield as a prospect, and the Reds have occasionally run him out at second and third this year, but they prefer to play him at first base. His versatility is occasionally valuable even now – he’s made four mid-game position switches in the last two months – but for the most part, he’s their everyday first baseman. That makes sense to me; that’s where our prospect team thought he’d end up, where scouts across the industry thought he’d end up, and where his team clearly thinks he’s the best fit.
I don’t believe the advanced metrics that say Stewart is a bad first base defender. It’s very hard to figure out defensive value at first base, and while Statcast thinks he’s below average at receiving throws, I’m not confident enough in their numbers, given the newness of the statistic and the few innings Stewart has played, to think he’s anything other than average. I bet he’ll improve over time, too; the Reds didn’t give him much playing time at first in the minors, so he’ll continue to learn on the job. But nevertheless, he’s not some defensive wizard out there.
That doesn’t matter all that much when it comes to my estimation of Stewart’s trajectory as a baseball player. He plays a position where they pay you to hit, and he hits. Sounds good to me. But you can have that in your head, and also say that on the defensive side of the ball, you’d prefer Wetherholt. Forget the magnitude for a minute – Gold Glove-contender second baseman or bat-first corner infielder looking for a defensive home. Leave their offense out of the comparison and weigh the two defensive profiles against each other, and there’s a clear winner.
Benge doesn’t fit quite as cleanly into the discussion here, so I left him for last. He’s a good right fielder, thanks in large part to his cannon arm; he’s thrown out 10 baserunners on the year. Generally speaking, I’d rather have an excellent second baseman than a good right fielder, but this is a closer call for me. To continue my analogizing to past Astros, I’d prefer Altuve (career 127 wRC+) to George Springer (career 128 wRC+). But defensive metrics are noisy, and if you thought Benge was just as good of a defender as Wetherholt, I’d disagree with you but wouldn’t think you were being unreasonable.
Where does that leave us? With a decision to make about how much we care about hitting, baserunning, and fielding. I can’t choose those weights for you. You might think that hitting is worth 30 times more than baserunning or fielding, or that baserunning is the most important by a mile. I think you’d be silly to think either, but your opinions are your own. I can, however, tell you my own views.
Of those three phases, hitting is the one I care about most. It’s the most stable, and you can stack up the most value there. Alvarez, the best hitter in baseball this year, checks in at 70 RE24. Crow-Armstrong, in one of the greatest defensive seasons of all time, is something like 25 runs above average in center. Witt is first in baseball in baserunning value, 8.5 runs above average. The ranges don’t lie.
But we’re not choosing between the best hitter in baseball and the best fielder in baseball. We’re choosing between a good-hitting first baseman, a solid-hitting second baseman who’s also a very good defender and baserunner, and a right fielder who does everything well. If Wetherholt were swinging a wet noodle out there, it wouldn’t matter how many double plays he turned or how many times he took the extra base. But heck, he got on base more frequently than Stewart this year in a tougher home park for offense, and he’s also approaching the 20-homer plateau. Benge is also right on the doorstep of 20 homers, and he’s similarly electric on the bases and no slouch in the field. They aren’t chopped liver.
For me, the decision is very close at the top – and it’s between Wetherholt and Benge. I’d put Stewart in third despite his enviable run production totals. I understand why Stewart is a leading contender despite WAR not liking his season. I think that people who say to completely ignore RBIs and batting average are missing the point. But I think that blindly taking RBI totals is just as bad as blindly taking WAR totals (worse, really, but both are bad). Context is important everywhere in life, and baseball is no exception. For me, the sum total of Wetherholt’s and Benge’s seasons across hitting, running, and fielding is better than Stewart’s in the same categories. I’d vote for Wetherholt, but I’ll level with you: I started this tale of the tape thinking it was a clear choice and ended it thinking that I’d be pretty happy voting for Benge too.
If you’re a voter reading this, I hope you take my advice into consideration and look at each candidate’s total contributions in context to make your decision. Like I said, I wouldn’t fault you for voting for Stewart if you think his performance at the plate is so staggering that the rest of it doesn’t matter. But if you’re just looking at the RBI total and going on that, I urge you to broaden your horizons just a little bit before making a choice. And if you’re a fan, well, there’s really no losing here. Any of these three would be deserving winners. I hope you enjoyed this comically long discussion of the most fascinating awards race of the season in any case.
Ben is a writer at FanGraphs. He can be found on Bluesky @benclemens.

Why Astros need to improve offense around Yordan Alvarez in 2027 originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
It's a borderline miracle the Houston Astros find themselves in their current position.
At 78-80, they are two games below .500 yet fighting to win the AL West and clinch an automatic berth to the ALDS.
That shouldn't be possible, yet here we are.
Houston's mediocrity paints a clear picture of the rest of the AL West, including the 78-80 Texas Rangers.
If the Astros managed to make a few more offensive additions at the trade deadline, they may be in full control of the division with less than a handful of games remaining.
But their offense around MVP candidate Yordan Alvarez has been one of the worst in baseball.
"Yordan Alvarez is challenging for the AL Triple Crown, hitting .314 with 41 home runs and 102 RBI. He is the heavy favorite for AL MVP honors even as the Astros fight for their playoff lives," Bleacher Report's Joel Reuter wrote.
Aside from Alvarez's 191 OPS+, the highest output in the lineup belongs to third baseman Isaac Paredes (126 OPS+).
"One of the biggest reasons they are still on the bubble, hovering around the .500 mark, is the complete lack of offensive consistency around Alvarez. A .687 OPS from the rest of the team tells the story," Reuter added.
Gone are the days when Jose Altuve can carry an offense for weeks at a time.
Plus, Daulton Varsho's lack of production (.535 OPS) in 41 games since a trade from the Toronto Blue Jays is not helping.
Houston's roster has a clear need this offseason.
Bats, more bats, and even more bats.

Mariners rally past Astros 6-5 in 10 innings to keep faint playoff hopes alive
Posted/updated on: September 24, 2026 at 6:59 am
SEATTLE (AP) — Josh Naylor singled home Randy Arozarena with the winning run in the 10th inning and the Seattle Mariners kept their slim playoff hopes alive by rallying past the Houston Astros 6-5 on Wednesday night.
Houston (78-80) remained tied atop the AL West with Texas, which has lost three straight games. The Astros hold the head-to-head tiebreaker if the teams finish with the same record.
The Mariners (74-84) are four games back with four to play.
Seattle was down 5-4 after automatic runner Yordan Alvarez scored on a triple to right field by Isaac Paredes in the top of the 10th.
With one out and the bases loaded in the bottom half, Julio Rodríguez worked a full-count walk from Astros closer Josh Hader, forcing in J.P. Crawford with the tying run. Naylor sent Hader’s next pitch to right-center, and Arozarena scored his third run of the night.
Alvarez went 2 for 4 without an RBI in his pursuit of the AL Triple Crown. That raised his league-leading batting average to .316. Tampa Bay’s Chandler Simpson, second at .309, did not play Wednesday against the New York Yankees.
Alvarez is part of a four-way tie for the home run lead at 41 with the Rays’ Junior Caminero, Baltimore’s Pete Alonso and the Yankees’ Ben Rice. The Houston slugger is second in RBIs with 102, eight behind Alonso.
Before his tying walk, Rodríguez had three hits for the Mariners.
Jose Altuve, Yainer Diaz and Nick Allen each had two hits for Houston. One of Diaz’s hits was his 14th homer, a two-run shot to cap a four-run third.
Cooper Criswell (4-2) pitched the 10th inning to earn the win for Seattle. Hader (4-2), who also pitched the ninth, took the loss.
Seattle scored three times in the third to pull to 4-3. The first two runs came on Dominic Canzone’s double as he extended his hitting streak to a career-best 12 games. Canzone’s single in the fifth scored Arozarena to tie it at 4.
Up next
The Mariners will send right-hander Bryan Woo (12-9, 3.92 ERA) to the mound Thursday in the opener of a season-ending four-game series against the Angels.
Right-hander Peter Lambert (8-10, 3.70) will pitch for the Astros in the first game of a four-game set at the Athletics.

Josh Naylor's walk-off single in 10th propels Mariners past Astros
(Photo credit: Joe Nicholson)
Josh Naylor lined a one-out single to center field with the bases loaded in the bottom of the 10th inning to score the deciding run as the Seattle Mariners kept their slim playoff hopes alive with a 6-5 victory against the visiting Houston Astros on Wednesday night.
Dominic Canzone drove in three runs for the Mariners (74-84), whose only chance to make the postseason is to finish in a three-way tie with Houston (78-80) and Texas (78-80), who are tied atop the American League West.
Yainer Diaz hit a tiebreaking triple in the top of the 10th inning after earlier hitting a two-run homer for the Astros.
Houston closer Josh Hader (4-2), who pitched the ninth, returned to the mound in the 10th to try and put the Astros into sole possession of the division lead. With J.P. Crawford the automatic runner, Hader walked Randy Arozarena before Canzone hit a slow roller to shortstop Nick Allen to advance both runners. A walk to Cal Raleigh loaded the bases and another to Julio Rodriguez forced in the tying run. Naylor lined the first pitch he saw from Hader up the middle to win it.
Mariners reliever Cooper Criswell (4-2) allowed one run on one hit with one strikeout in one inning.
The Astros opened the scoring with four runs in the top of the third off Mariners starter George Kirby. With one out, Allen doubled to left. Jose Altuve hit what turned out to be a single down the left-field line that deflected off third-base umpire Ryan Blakney's shin. Yordan Alvarez doubled to right, sending Altuve to third, before Isaac Paredes lifted a sacrifice fly to right. Diaz then lined a two-run shot over the left-field wall to make it 4-0.
The Mariners responded with three runs in the bottom of the inning against Astros starter Ethan Pecko. Lazaro Montes drew a leadoff walk and, an out later, Crawford grounded a single to right. Both runners advanced on a wild pitch. Arozarena walked to load the bases for Canzone, who lined a two-run single off the right-field wall. With two outs, Rodriguez lined a double to left to cut Houston's lead to 4-3.
The Mariners tied it in the fifth off reliever Josh Hendrickson, who was making his MLB debut. Arozarena lined a one-out single to center, stole second and scored on Canzone's single to center.
Pecko pitched 2 2/3 innings and gave up three runs on four hits. The rookie right-hander walked two and struck out two.
Kirby went five innings and allowed four runs on six hits. The right-hander walked three and fanned five.
--Field Level Media

item.content:encoded:
Field Level Media

23 Sep 2026, 12:25 GMT+10

(Photo credit: Brad Penner)
Drew Rasmussen allowed one hit in 6 2/3 outstanding innings and the visiting Tampa Bay Rays clinched the American League East with a 6-1 victory over the New York Yankees on Tuesday night in the nightcap of a day-night doubleheader.
The Rays won for the 20th time in 28 games and clinched their fifth division title. Tampa Bay last won the AL East in 2021 when it won a team-record 100 games. Yandy Diaz drove in four runs on a pair of singles.
Rasmussen (16-5) took a no-hitter into the seventh until Heliot Ramos opened the inning with a double to left for New York. Ramos eventually scored on an RBI single by rookie George Lombard Jr. off Kevin Kelly.
Rasmussen finished with 11 strikeouts for his fourth career double-digit strikeout performance. He finished two shy of his career-high set June 10 against the Boston Red Sox and the Rays won his 12th consecutive start.
Yankees 2, Rays 0 (Game 1)
Cody Bellinger hit a two-run home run in the fourth inning as host New York recorded a shutout over Tampa Bay in the opener of a day-night doubleheader.
With the victory, the Yankees temporarily prevented the Rays from clinching the AL East and moved six games ahead of the Boston Red Sox for the American League's top wild-card spot.
New York's Carlos Rodon (7-3) scattered three singles over eight innings as the Yankees finished off the victory in a brisk 2 hours, 2 minutes. Rodon struck out eight in his 100th career win and also reached 1,500 strikeouts for his career. Rays right-hander Nick Martinez (15-5) allowed two runs on five hits over six innings with seven strikeouts to take his first loss since July 9.
Dodgers 7, Padres 0
Freddie Freeman drove in three runs, Will Smith and Tommy Edman hit home runs, and Los Angeles inched closer to the best record in the National League with a shutout of visiting San Diego.
Eight Dodgers pitchers held down the red-hot Padres offense in a bullpen game, with Justin Wrobleski (12-5) earning the win. Roki Sasaki struck out two in one inning in his return from a blister issue. The Dodgers extended their home winning streak to 11 games.
Los Angeles moved to within one game of the NL-best Milwaukee Brewers and reduced its magic number for a top-two NL spot and a bye into the National League Division Series to one. Luis Campusano had two hits for the Padres, whose magic number to clinch a playoff spot remained at two.
Phillies 6, Brewers 4
Bryson Stott delivered the tiebreaking hit in the eighth inning to guide Philadelphia to a victory over visiting Milwaukee. Brandon Marsh homered and knocked in three runs as the Phillies lowered their magic number to two to clinch a postseason berth.
Zack Wheeler ended up with a no-decision after striking out 11 while giving up three runs and five hits in 5 2/3 innings. Wheeler struck out the first seven batters he faced, setting a Phillies record for consecutive strikeouts to begin a game. His first-inning strikeout of Brice Turang was the 2,000th of his career.
The Brewers saw their lead over the Dodgers for the top record in the majors shrink to one as they lost just the third time in their last 13 games. William Contreras knocked in three runs.
Marlins 8, Cubs 2 (12 innings)
Griffin Conine plated the go-ahead run that ignited a six-run 12th inning for visiting Miami, which snapped a three-game losing by beating Chicago and postponing the Cubs' playoff celebration for at least a day.
On a night when runs were scarce until the final inning, both teams endured a pair of scoreless extra frames before Conine broke the drought with a leadoff, golf-shot single off Caleb Thielbar that fell just inside the left field line. Esteury Ruiz, the automatic runner, scored from second to make it 3-2 as the Marlins sent 10 batters to the plate in the inning.
The Cubs could have clinched a wild-card playoff spot with a win or Arizona loss, but neither of those happened keeping the Diamondbacks mathematically alive. Josh Ekness (3-4) struck out a pair in the 11th inning to get the win while Thielbar (3-4) gave up three runs -- two earned -- in his inning of work.
Guardians 3, Red Sox 2
Nathaniel Lowe drove in Chase DeLauter with a sacrifice fly in the ninth inning and Cleveland held on to beat host Boston in the first game of a three-game series.
Cleveland not only extended its winning streak to six but maintained its one-game lead over the Chicago White Sox for first place in the AL Central.
Parker Messick held Boston to one run on five hits in five innings, his 14th straight start allowing three runs or fewer. Payton Tolle started for the Red Sox and gave up two runs on eight hits in 5 2/3 innings as the Guardians went 1-for-12 with runners in scoring position and stranded 15.
White Sox 14, Royals 11
Chase Meidroth smacked a three-run home run among his three hits and drove in five, and Brenton Doyle, Randal Grichuk and Munetaka Murakami also homered to power Chicago past host Kansas City.
Chicago won for the fourth time in five games to remain one game behind the AL Central-leading Cleveland Guardians. The White Sox, who hold the third and final AL wild-card spot, reduced their magic number to earn a playoff berth to three.
Vinnie Pasquantino hit a ninth-inning grand slam for the Royals, who lost their fifth straight. He went 3-for-5 with a double and also drove in five.
Nationals 3, Tigers 1
CJ Abrams hit a pair of home runs and drove in all three runs as visiting Washington topped Detroit. Abrams reached 100 RBIs for the season with his solo shot in the second inning, then broke a 1-1 tie in the seventh with his 33rd long ball of the season, a two-run blast.
Dylan Crews had two hits and scored the other run for the Nationals. Rookie Jackson Kent (2-4) earned the win in long relief. He allowed one run on six hits over four innings and struck out three. Opener Riley Cornelio lasted 2 2/3 innings, striking out four and walking three.
Ben Malgeri scored the Tigers' only run. Kevin McGonigle and Max Clark each had two hits.
Pirates 2, Cardinals 0
Jared Jones and two relievers combined on a one-hitter as Pittsburgh beat visiting St. Louis for a fifth straight win. Jones (5-6) lowered his ERA to 1.08 in four September starts and struck out nine with zero walks over seven innings while throwing 63 of his 86 pitches for strikes.
Pittsburgh broke a scoreless tie with two outs in the sixth inning on Ryan O'Hearn's RBI single against Andre Pallante (12-8). Pallante allowed one run on three hits with two walks and two strikeouts over six innings.
St. Louis struck out 14 times and lost for the fifth time in its last six games.
Astros 7, Mariners 0
Christian Walker hit a three-run home run, Yordan Alvarez launched a two-run homer and Isaac Paredes added a solo shot as Houston slugged and pitched its way past host Seattle.
Jose Altuve, Yainer Diaz, Alvarez and Paredes each collected two hits for the Astros, who pulled into a first-place tie with the Texas Rangers in the West. Five Astros pitchers combined to throw a four-hit shutout. Miguel Ullola (1-0) earned his first major league win, allowing one hit and striking out two over two innings of relief.
Julio Rodriguez notched two hits for Seattle. The Mariners went 0-for-3 with runners in scoring position and stranded nine.
Reds 4, Braves 0
Brandon Williamson fired six scoreless innings and Cincinnati supported him with three solo homers to defeat host Atlanta in the opener of a three-game series.
Cincinnati ended a two-game losing streak and evened the season series with Atlanta at 2-2. Williamson (5-4) worked six scoreless innings, allowing three hits and two strikeouts. Elly De La Cruz (29), Dane Myers (8) and Eugenio Suarez (25) each hit a home run for the Reds. It was Suarez's 350th career homer, making him the 10th active player to reach that mark.
Atlanta starter JR Ritchie (1-4) pitched five innings and allowed one run on four hits and three walks. The rookie struck out a career-high eight batters.
Mets 6, Rangers 3
Francisco Alvarez laced a go-ahead two-run double in the sixth, then scored an insurance run on an unusual sacrifice fly for visiting New York, who damaged Texas' playoff hopes with a win in the opener of a three-game interleague series in Arlington.
Juan Soto had an RBI single in the third, and Carson Benge capped the scoring with a run-scoring double in the seventh for the Mets. The club won hours after removing the interim tag from manager Andy Green and signing him to a three-year extension.
Josh Jung had an RBI double in the third, and Elias Diaz and Wyatt Langford lofted sacrifice flies in the fourth for the Rangers, who entered Tuesday with a one-game lead over the Houston Astros in the AL West.
Diamondbacks 7, Rockies 2
Nolan Arenado homered and doubled among his three hits, Michael Soroka tossed seven strong innings, and Arizona kept its slim postseason hopes alive with a win over host Colorado in Denver.
Geraldo Perdomo also had three hits and Ildemaro Vargas finished with two hits for Arizona, which remains alive in the NL wild-card race, sitting four games behind Philadelphia, San Diego and the Chicago Cubs for the third and final spot with five games to go.
Mickey Moniak homered for Colorado, which finished with just three hits and just one after the third inning. The Rockies (57-100) are the first team to lose 100 or more games in four straight seasons since the 1962-65 New York Mets.
Twins 3, Giants 2
Walker Jenkins homered, Luke Keaschall contributed both offensively and defensively, and Minnesota evened its road interleague series against San Francisco.
Taj Bradley (12-6) combined with four relievers on a six-hitter for the Twins, who used two late diving catches by Keaschall in right field to prevent the Giants from taking the first two of the series.
Bradley allowed just one other hit -- a fifth-inning single by Drew Gilbert -- in his six innings. He walked three and struck out six. Keaschall's one-out triple scored Ryan Kreidler, then Brooks Lee gave Minnesota the lead for good with a run-scoring single to plate Keaschall.
A's 9, Angels 7
Carlos Cortes hit a go-ahead two-run homer in the bottom of the eighth inning and the Athletics overcame a six-run deficit to beat Los Angeles in West Sacramento, Calif.
In addition to the homer off Sam Bachman, Cortes also delivered a pinch-hit RBI triple in the seventh, helping the Athletics end a six-game losing streak. Zack Gelof hit a two-run homer later in the eighth for the A's. Shea Langeliers and Lawrence Butler each had three hits and an RBI for the Athletics.
Denzer Guzman homered and drove in four RBIs for the Angels, who have lost four of their last six games. Mike Trout added three hits and two runs for Los Angeles (60-97), which has never lost 100 games in a season.
Blue Jays at Orioles, ppd.
The scheduled game between Toronto and host Baltimore was postponed due to ongoing inclement weather. The game will be made up as part of a split doubleheader on Wednesday, with games starting at 1:35 p.m. and 6:35 p.m. ET.
--Field Level Media

Injuries have started to take a toll on the Toronto Blue Jays lately. While it seemed like there was still hope for Toronto to make the postseason a couple of weeks ago, that has ultimately not turned out to be the case.
The struggles have been real, and the injuries have not made it easier. Outfielder Brett Bateman suffered a hip injury on Monday night, while first baseman Vladimir Guerrero Jr. has dealt with back tightness. Not to mention starter Trey Yesavage, who just returned from knee surgery after six weeks.
Ace Dylan Cease had been holding down the rotation recently, but even he hasn't been immune to the injury bug that has hurt the Blue Jays this season. Cease has been a lifeline to Toronto's pitching staff, but had been dealing with shoulder fatigue over the past few weeks, according to manager John Schneider.
Cease struggled mightily against the Texas Rangers on Friday, going just 2.2 innings and walking six, while giving up four runs (one earned). He went back to Toronto for an MRI and was scratched from his next start on Wednesday.
It was revealed on Monday that the MRI only showed inflammation in the right shoulder and no structural issues. Cease will not need surgery for anything more serious.
More on Cease's Injury Situation
The 30-year-old explained the news himself and the fact that he's just been diagnosed with shoulder inflammation. This isn't an issue that is expected to go into 2027 and affect his availability for next season.
It's still unlikely that Cease ends up pitching again this season with less than a week left, although that's still being determined. Given the Jays are basically out of postseason contention, there's really no need to push him.
The shoulder issue is what caused Cease's pitch velocity to go down.
“The velocity being down has been a little bit concerning,” Cease said, according to Keegan Matheson of MLB.com. "But at the same time, I’m getting outs. It wasn’t anything that was too scary because nothing about it feels like I’ve got something that needs surgery."
After his incredible complete game at the Boston Red Sox on July 25, where he threw 120 pitches, Cease didn't look as strong, even though he still ended up throwing six quality starts from that time until now.
“It’s definitely a bit heavy and achy, just not normal,” Cease said. "The last couple of starts, the velo keeps going down and down. Especially that last one, I almost felt like I was hurting the team."
It's clear that the issue caught him to him, but the fact that he pitched through it at a high level for some time shows the quality of Cease.
He has posted a 2.40 ERA in 29 starts, which is the second-lowest mark in the American League. Cease has a career-high 239 strikeouts in 169 innings pitched, with an 11-6 record.

Ronald Acuña Jr. suma su tercera temporada con al menos 20 jonrones y 20 bases robadas en MLB y entra al top 3 entre venezolanos.
Ronald Acuña Jr. sigue escribiendo su nombre en la historia del béisbol venezolano. El outfielder de los Bravos de Atlanta cerró otra temporada con al menos 20 jonrones y 20 bases robadas, un logro que pocos han repetido con tanta consistencia. Acuña alcanza su tercera campaña 20-20 y con eso se suma a un grupo selecto de compatriotas que marcaron época en Grandes Ligas.
El camino no fue sencillo. Las lesiones interrumpieron su ritmo en varios momentos y limitaron su presencia en la alineación. Aun así, el criollo encontró la forma de producir cuando estuvo disponible y dejó números que respaldan su calidad. Su combinación de poder y velocidad lo mantiene como una pieza clave en el ataque de Atlanta y como referencia obligada al hablar de los mejores peloteros de Venezuela.
Este hito llega en un año en el que muchos dudaban de su capacidad para mantener el nivel de años anteriores y en el que las lesiones volvieron a estar presentes. Pese a esto los números de Acuña confirman su recuperación, algo que resulta clave tomando en cuenta que nos acercamos a octubre y que Atlanta lo necesita sano para poder pelear en playoffs.
MÁS INFORMACIÓN: Ronald Acuña Jr.: velocidad, poder y una nueva página en MLB
Qué significa la temporada 20-20 de Ronald Acuña Jr. en 2026
Una campaña 20-20 exige un buen desempeño en dos facetas claves de la ofensiva: pegarle fuerte a la bola y saber correr las bases con inteligencia. Acuña cumplió con ese doble requisito en 2026 y con eso llegó a su tercera temporada 20-20 en la MLB. Sus otras dos veces con al menos 20 jonrones y 20 bases robadas llegaron en 2019 y 2023, años en los que también dejó un perfil ofensivo completo, con poder en el bate y presión en las bases.
Acuña acumula 103 partidos en 2026, con 454 apariciones en el plato, 102 hits, 55 carreras impulsadas y 60 anotadas. Esos números reflejan un rendimiento sólido para un jugador que pasó por dos distensiones en el corva izquierda y que en varios tramos de la temporada no estuvo al 100%. Aun con esos obstáculos, el criollo fue capaz de dejar muy buenos números en esta temporada regular.
Este tipo de registro no depende solo de fuerza. También exige una excelente lectura de lanzamientos, disciplina en el plato y timing para robar algo que lo ha caracterizado a lo largo de su carrera. Hay que recordar que Acuña suma 225 bases robadas de por vida y 206 jonrones en su carrera regular, cifras que lo ubican en un nivel distinto dentro de la ofensiva venezolana en la MLB.
El club selecto de venezolanos con temporadas 20-20 en MLB
Pocos peloteros de Venezuela han logrado una campaña 20-20. El grupo lo encabezan Bobby Abreu, Carlos González y José Altuve, tres nombres que definieron épocas distintas y que dejaron huella en sus respectivas franquicias. Acuña se une a ese trío y con su tercera vez se ubica en el top 3 histórico de jonroneros venezolanos en Grandes Ligas, un escalón que pocos alcanzan y que mide impacto real en el juego.
Bobby Abreu marcó el estándar con la marca 20-20 en 9 temporadas a lo largo de su carrera en MLB, un número que refleja su combinación de poder y velocidad durante más de una década. Carlos González alcanzó ese registro en 4 ocasiones durante sus 12 campañas en la liga mayor, con picos de producción que lo llevaron a la élite del bateo. José Altuve, por su parte, suma 3 temporadas 20-20 con los Astros de Houston, un logro que respalda su perfil de bateador de contacto con velocidad en las bases.
La marca de Acuña también tiene un componente de resistencia. Llegar tres veces a 20-20 implica mantener salud relativa y rendimiento en distintos momentos de la carrera. El criollo ya tiene un MVP en 2023, un Rookie del Año en 2018 y un récord histórico de 40-70 en esa misma campaña del MVP. Esos logros, sumados a su tercera temporada 20-20, lo convierten en referencia para la nueva generación de peloteros venezolanos.

- Carlos González (4)
- Ronald Acuña Jr. (3)
- Jackson Chourio (3)

- Elvis Andrus (1)

Por qué Ronald Acuña Jr. sigue siendo clave para los Bravos y para Venezuela
Atlanta construye su ataque alrededor de la versatilidad. Acuña ofrece poder desde la parte alta del orden al bate, capacidad para estirar hits y presión constante sobre la defensa rival. Esa combinación hace que su presencia en el lineup, incluso con minutos limitados debido a las lesiones, cambie la dinámica del juego.
Acuña apenas tiene 28 años y ya suma tres campañas 20-20, una cifra que deja espacio para seguir creciendo. Su historial de poder y velocidad, sumado a su capacidad de ajuste, lo pone en ruta para añadir más temporadas con al menos 20 jonrones y 20 bases robadas. La gran incógnita ahora es si podrá igualar o superar las 9 veces de Bobby Abreu, el récord entre venezolanos en MLB. El tiempo dirá si el criollo se acerca a esa marca o si incluso la deja atrás.
